description.value: This study examined brain responses to visual food cues in healthy pre-pubertal children and their relationships with adiposity and sex.

value: We hypothesized that viewing food vs. non-food cues would be associated with increased brain activity in regions involved in reward, taste, conditioned responses to food, and visual and attention processing.
we hypothesized differential engagement of brain regions involved in processing food cues between children with greater adiposity vs. smaller adiposity.
we hypothesized that girls (relative to boys) may exhibit greater brain food cue reactivity.

description.value: Observational, cross-sectional study of healthy pre-pubertal children.

spans.text: In this study, we investigated patterns of brain food cue responsivity in a cohort of healthy, typically developing pre-pubertal children between the ages of 7 and 11 years.
Whole-brain analysis of food vs. non-food contrast

definition.value: Viewing pictures of food vs. non-food cues was associated with increased BOLD signal change.

spans.text: Viewing pictures of food vs. non-food cues was associated with increased BOLD signal change in the bilateral ventral striatum, putamen/pallidum, caudate, insula, amygdala, hippocampus, occipital cortex, parietal cortex, thalamus, hypothalamus, precentral gyrus, postcentral gyrus, OFC, ACC, posterior cingulate cortex, medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), brain stem and left frontal pole ( Figure 1 , Table 2 ).
Fifty-three pre-pubertal children (age: 8.18 ± 0.66 years; sex: 22 boys, 31 girls) were included in the final neuroimaging data analysis.

Viewing pictures of food vs. non-food cues was associated with increased BOLD signal change in the bilateral ventral striatum, putamen/pallidum, caudate, insula, amygdala, hippocampus, occipital cortex, parietal cortex, thalamus, hypothalamus, precentral gyrus, postcentral gyrus, OFC, ACC, posterior cingulate cortex, medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), brain stem and left frontal pole ( Figure 1 , Table 2 ).
Food cues consisted of palatable food items such as cupcakes and French fries.

Viewing pictures of food vs. non-food cues was associated with increased BOLD signal change in the bilateral ventral striatum, putamen/pallidum, caudate, insula, amygdala, hippocampus, occipital cortex, parietal cortex, thalamus, hypothalamus, precentral gyrus, postcentral gyrus, OFC, ACC, posterior cingulate cortex, medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), brain stem and left frontal pole ( Figure 1 , Table 2 ).
The control stimuli consisted of non-food neutral pictures such as books and rulers.

Whole-brain analysis results of food vs. non-food contrast, whole-brain regression analysis relating individual differences in percent body fat to food vs. non-food contrast adjusting for age and sex, and unpaired- t test results of boys relative to girls for food vs. non-food contrast (cluster level correction, Z>2.3, P<.05).
Based on prior studies conducted in similar age range as our participants 15 , 30 , we used the Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI) template for registration.
